questions.q: While editing a formula, pressing F4 on the reference A1 changes it to:
questions.solution: F4 cycles the reference through A1 -> $A$1 -> A$1 -> $A1 -> A1. The first press makes it fully absolute.
questions.shortcut: One tap of F4 = full lock ($ before both letter and number).

questions.q: In the URL https://www.ssc.gov.in, the component '.in' is the:
questions.solution: .in is the country-code top-level domain for India. 'https' is the protocol, 'www' the sub-domain/host, 'ssc' the registered domain name.
questions.shortcut: Read right to left: .in = TLD, .gov = second level, ssc = the name.

questions.q: How many links are needed for a full mesh topology with 5 computers?
questions.shortcut: Five nodes -> 5x4/2; the 20 option is the un-halved trap for those using n(n-1) with n=5... actually 20 = n x (n-1), another halving slip - always divide by 2.

questions.q: In Windows File Explorer, which shortcut creates a new folder in the current location?
questions.solution: Ctrl+Shift+N creates a new folder in Explorer. Plain Ctrl+N opens a new Explorer window. In Chrome, Ctrl+Shift+N opens an incognito window.
questions.shortcut: Ctrl+N = new window; add Shift for a new folder.

questions.q: Each option is a fragment of a different sentence. Exactly one fragment contains an error. Select it.
options: The commander-in-chief, with his soldiers, was
Each of the participants have received
The poet and philosopher has written
Ten kilometres is a long walk
questions.solution: **Each** of the participants → singular → each **has** received. 'With his soldiers' leaves the first noun as subject, 'the poet and philosopher' names one person (has), and a distance as one unit takes *is* — all correct.
questions.shortcut: each of → singular; with-phrase is a decoy.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
questions.solution: The advice sentence ends 'give the water ten patient sessions before you judge yourself'. The surrounding lines — Meena learnt at thirty-eight; the coach preached patience — build one message: age must not decide whether an adult tries. So: '**ignore** your age'. *Count* is the tempting opposite (age is a number), but the passage never asks anyone to calculate; it asks them to start.
questions.shortcut: Read the lines before and after the blank: patience and a 38-year-old learner point to one instruction.
questions.passage: Meena learnt to swim at thirty-eight, two years after her daughter did. At the first class she held the pool edge so hard that her fingers ached, and she (1) ______ the deep end as if it were a border between two countries. Her coach, a retired lifeguard, refused to teach strokes at first; for a week she only walked in the shallow water and blew bubbles. 'Fear leaves through the body, not the (2) ______,' he told her when she asked for a book on techniques. By the third month she could float, and floating, she says, changed everything: the moment the water held her, she stopped fighting it. Last month she swam the pool's full length, and her daughter, who once (3) ______ her from the gallery, now swims beside her. Meena's advice to adults is simple: begin this month, (4) ______ your age, and give the water ten patient sessions before you judge yourself.

questions.q: The phrase 'turn bedrooms into ovens' in the passage conveys that the rooms:
options: are well ventilated but poorly lit
are used for cooking at night
become unbearably hot to sleep in
questions.solution: The phrase is figurative: tin roofs under which the poorest residents live make bedrooms extremely hot, so hot that sleep is impossible — the oven image conveys unbearable heat. Literal readings — cooking or actual ovens in bedrooms — are the bait; ventilation/lighting is not discussed at all.
questions.shortcut: Phrase-in-context = treat as one figurative unit; reject any option that reads the words literally.
questions.passage:
Cities are quietly getting hotter than the countryside that surrounds them, and the gap is measured every night. On a summer evening, a village a few kilometres outside a metropolis may cool to a comfortable twenty-six degrees while the city itself still holds thirty-three. This difference, known as the urban heat island effect, arises not from global warming alone but from the way cities are built. Concrete, asphalt and brick absorb solar energy all day and release it slowly after sunset, so the city never truly cools. Fewer trees mean less shade and less of the cooling that water escaping from leaves provides. Waste heat from air conditioners, vehicles and industry adds a further burden.

The consequences fall unevenly. The poorest residents often live in dense, poorly ventilated neighbourhoods with tin roofs that turn bedrooms into ovens, and they cannot afford the electricity that cooling demands. Studies in several Indian cities have linked heat waves to falling productivity among construction and delivery workers, whose shifts rarely move to the cooler hours. Night-time heat is particularly dangerous because sleep is when the body repairs itself; hospitals report more admissions during hot nights even when the days seem tolerable.

Solutions need not wait for global action. Painting roofs white, mandating reflective materials for new construction, restoring ponds and planting street trees can lower local temperatures measurably within a single season. Ahmedabad's heat action plan, which pairs early warnings with cool-roof subsidies, has become a model studied by other developing countries. What these measures share is a simple insight: heat islands are created by design choices, and design choices can be remade. The city that planned itself into a heat trap can plan itself out of one.

questions.q: The tone of the passage is:
questions.solution: The passage only explains three scientific reasons and one exception. There are no jokes, no faults pointed out and no fond memories of the past — it simply informs.
questions.shortcut: Facts + explanation + no evaluative words = informative/neutral.
questions.passage: Honey does not spoil easily because of three properties. It contains very little water, so the microbes that cause decay cannot grow in it. It is slightly acidic. And bees add an enzyme that slowly produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, a substance that kills germs. If honey is left open to damp air, however, it can absorb moisture and begin to ferment.

questions.q: The capital of the **Satavahana** kingdom was —
questions.solution: The Satavahanas ruled from **Pratishthana (Paithan)** on the Godavari (Maharashtra). Vatapi = Chalukyas of Badami; Manyakheta = Rashtrakutas; Kanchipuram = Pallavas.

questions.q: Which country topped the medal table at the Commonwealth Games 2026?
questions.solution: Australia topped the table for the third consecutive Games with 70 gold and 171 total medals.
questions.shortcut: Australia has topped every CWG medal table since 2006 except Birmingham 2022's tie context — default answer.

questions.q: The Durand Line forms the boundary between:
questions.solution: The **Durand Line** (1893, drawn by Sir Mortimer Durand) marks the **Pakistan–Afghanistan** border. India–China is the McMahon Line and India–Pakistan is the Radcliffe Line.

questions.q: Who discovered the neutron?
questions.solution: **James Chadwick** discovered the neutron in **1932** (Nobel Prize 1935). Thomson discovered the electron and Rutherford the atomic nucleus.
questions.shortcut: 'Tom Ran Chasing' — the third particle goes to Chadwick.

questions.q: Find the LCM of 0.12, 0.18 and 0.30.
questions.solution:
Clear decimals (× 100): 12, 18, 30 → LCM $= 180$.
Two decimal places → answer $= 1.80$.
Check: $1.8 \div 0.12 = 15$, $1.8 \div 0.18 = 10$, $1.8 \div 0.30 = 6$ — all whole ✓.

questions.q: Find the greatest number which divides 70, 110 and 150 leaving the same remainder in each case. What is that remainder?
questions.solution:
Pairwise differences: $110 - 70 = 40$, $150 - 110 = 40$, $150 - 70 = 80$.
HCF of differences $= 40$. Remainder $= 70 \bmod 40 = 30$ (same for 110 and 150 ✓).

questions.q: Find the compound interest on ₹8,000 at 20% per annum for 1$\frac{1}{2}$ years, compounded half-yearly.
questions.solution:
Rate per half-year = 10%; periods = 3.
$A = 8000 \times (1.1)^3 = 10648$, so CI = ₹2,648.

questions.q: By selling a table for ₹460 a trader gains 15%. The cost price of the table is:

Select the number that can replace the question mark (?) in the following series.

**2, 3, 7, 16, ?, 57**
questions.solution: Differences on the left: 1, 4, 9 (squares) → the next gaps are 16 and 25. ? = 16 + 16 = **32**. Check: 32 + 25 = 57 ✓.
questions.shortcut: Gap after ? must be the next square: 57 − 32 = 25 ✓.

questions.q:
Select the letter that can replace the question mark (?) in the following series.

**B, E, D, G, F, I, ?**
Select the related letters: **? : FDW :: DOG : GRJ**
questions.solution: GRJ is DOG with every letter moved **+3** (D→G, O→R, G→J). So ? = FDW moved **−3**: F→C, D→A, W→T → **CAT**.
questions.shortcut: Blank on the left: apply the discovered tuple backwards (subtract 3).

questions.q:
**Statement:** Advertisement: 'Learn to swim in just 15 days — join our summer swimming camp!'

**Assumptions:**
I. Some people want to learn swimming in a short time.
II. Nobody can learn swimming in less than 15 days.

Which of the assumptions is/are implicit in the statement?
options: Both I and II are implicit
Neither I nor II is implicit
questions.solution: I: the '15 days' pitch only attracts customers if people value quick learning — negate it and the advert loses its point, so I is **implicit**. II: the camp need not believe faster learning is impossible; it only claims 15 days is enough — **not implicit**. Answer: **Only I**.
questions.shortcut: An advert assumes its hook appeals to someone; it assumes nothing about rivals.
